name: Chlormadinone acetate pill

card.summary: A European antiandrogenic progestin in combined birth-control pills, used for acne in some countries with little published acne-specific trial data found.
card.note: Prescription-only; not sold in the US, UK, Canada or Australia.

quick.overview:
Chlormadinone acetate is a progestin with antiandrogen activity, combined with ethinylestradiol in pills such as Belara. It is used for contraception and for androgen-related skin conditions in countries where it is sold.

No acne-specific trials turned up in the sources reviewed; registered studies concern weight change and PCOS.
quick.mechanism: It blocks androgen receptors (about 30 to 40 percent of cyproterone acetate affinity) and suppresses LH and FSH, lowering testosterone.
quick.risks: Menstrual irregularity, headache, nausea and breast tenderness; contraindicated in pregnancy. Prescription only and unavailable in several countries including the US.

lead: Chlormadinone acetate (CMA) is a synthetic progestin with antiandrogenic activity, used with ethinylestradiol in combined oral contraceptives such as Belara, sold in Germany and Brazil among other countries.[1] Because it blocks androgen receptors and lowers LH and FSH, such pills are used in some countries to improve androgen-dependent skin and hair symptoms in women, including acne and hirsutism, which is why they appear in discussion of clearer skin.[1]

Wikipedia's drug summary states that combined pills containing CMA can reduce androgen-dependent skin and hair symptoms, and that CMA is marketed in much of Europe, Latin America and parts of Asia but not in the US, UK, Canada or Australia.[1] Published trial information specific to acne is limited: registered studies compare body-weight change on Belara versus a drospirenone pill and examine hormonal contraceptives in polycystic ovary syndrome, but neither is an acne trial.[2][3]

chain: CMA blocks androgen receptors and lowers LH and FSH
Lower androgen activity in skin and hair follicles
Fewer androgen-driven acne lesions and less hirsutism
angle.text: In countries where it is sold, a CMA-containing combined pill is prescribed for contraception and for androgen-related acne and excess hair growth in women. The skin benefit comes from reduced androgen signalling rather than a direct skin action.

infobox: Prescription only; not marketed in the US, UK, Canada or Australia

paras: Combined with ethinylestradiol, CMA is used for contraception and is also described as used for acne, hirsutism and other androgen-dependent conditions.[1] Separately from the pill, CMA has been used alone in gynaecological disorders, menopausal hot flashes and, in men, prostate conditions.[1] It is sold alone in France, Germany, Japan, Mexico and South Korea.[1]

CMA is a progesterone receptor agonist and an androgen receptor antagonist with about 30 to 40 percent of the receptor affinity of cyproterone acetate, and acts as a weak partial agonist. It also suppresses LH and FSH, lowering testosterone and estradiol.[1] Oral bioavailability is reported as about 100 percent, with 96.6 to 99.4 percent protein binding.[1]

CMA was discovered in 1959 and introduced medically in 1965. It was withdrawn in the US and UK around 1970 after mammary tumors appeared in beagle dogs at high doses; later research found no comparable risk in humans.[1]

With low-dose combined pills, reported effects include menstrual irregularities, headache (37 percent), nausea (23 percent) and breast tenderness (22 percent).[1] Wikipedia reports no liver function abnormalities in women taking combined pills containing CMA, one hepatocellular carcinoma case report, and that CMA does not increase the risk of venous thromboembolism.[1] It is contraindicated in pregnancy, and in menopausal therapy combined with estrogen it has been linked to increased breast cancer risk.[1]

No acne-specific trials were found. Registered studies include a phase 4 comparison of body-weight change during contraception with Belara versus Yasmin (n=100) and a study of the safety of hormonal contraceptive therapies in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (n=75).[2][3]

timeline.event: Withdrawn in the US and UK after dog mammary tumor findings.[1]
